content_metadata.description: A video comparing binaural hearing and single-sided deafness (SSD) through a series of demonstrations in a restaurant setting, highlighting the auditory experiences and challenges.

qAndA.answer: They are meeting for the first time. Man 1 explains he went to college with the other man (Peter) at the table.
qAndA.question: In the first restaurant scene (binaural hearing), what is the relationship between the blonde woman (Woman 1) and the man she's talking to (Man 1)?

qAndA.answer: It shows how someone with SSD might struggle to hear someone approaching from their deaf side, making social interaction and awareness difficult.
qAndA.question: What difficulty does the single-sided deafness simulation highlight when the waiter (Man 2) approaches the table?

qAndA.answer: He misses the question: "But isn't there a later movie too?" which impacts his understanding of the movie plans.
qAndA.question: In the conversation with the three friends (Woman 2, Man 1, Woman 3), what is the specific question that the man (Man 1) misses when the audio is muffled (simulating SSD)?

qAndA.answer: He briefly glances at Woman 3, as if trying to gauge her reaction or seek confirmation of what was said.
qAndA.question: During the second SSD simulation (Scene 4), what visual cue suggests that Man 1 is having trouble following the conversation, aside from the muffled audio?

qAndA.answer: The ending is intentionally abrupt, cutting off mid-conversation during the SSD simulation. This creates a lingering sense of frustration and highlights the constant challenges faced by individuals with SSD. The call to action then encourages viewers to learn more and seek solutions, ending on a hopeful but realistic note.
qAndA.question: What is the overall mood and message conveyed by the video's ending?

youtube_description:
What happens when you can only hear with one ear? This hearing loss in only one ear is often known as unilateral hearing loss or single-sided deafness. Check out our in-depth article on SSD here: https://blog.medel.pro/binaural-hearing-cochlear-implant-single-sided-deafness/

MED-EL cochlear implants are now approved for single-sided deafness in the United States! Learn more: https://hearlife.medel.com/en-us/cochlear-implants-for-single-sided-deafness

Hearing with both ears is known as binaural hearing. In this video, we look at the effect of hearing with both ears vs. hearing with only one ear.

Even with good hearing in the other ear, this hearing loss can make it very difficult to understand conversations in noise or tell where sounds are coming from. 

Want to know more about the science of the head shadow effect? Check out this article on our MED-EL Blog: https://blog.medel.com/head-shadow-effect-cochlear-implants/

Read a hearing therapist's experience with a cochlear implant & single-sided deafness: https://blog.medel.com/a-hearing-therapist-chose-med-el-for-single-sided-deafness-ssd/
 
If you have hearing loss in one ear or both ears, we recommend you see a hearing specialist to find the best treatment option for you.

MED-EL is the leading innovator in the field of hearing implants. We help others hear the joys of sound through groundbreaking technologies. MED-EL products are made at our headquarters in Austria and we are helping people overcome hearing loss in more than 100 countries. To learn more about our passion for helping people with hearing loss go to http://www.medel.com.



*This video is not meant to simulate how a recipient of a MED-EL hearing implant will hear.
youtube_title: Hearing With Only One Ear: Binaural Hearing vs. Unilateral Hearing Loss
